title: On Govt agenda: New Rs 2,800-cr capex scheme for critical minerals
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Infrastructure: energy; Mobilisation of resources · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources across the world and India · GS2 › Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (China) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
summary: The Union Cabinet is likely to take up a scheme of about Rs 2,800 crore that offers a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, to build India's domestic critical mineral processing base.
evolution: PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal; storage needs batteries (energy thread).
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: The gap is processing, not only mining: India has little processing capacity and is almost fully import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
GS3 · Industry / GS1 · Resources
India's critical mineral weakness lies in processing; mining ore is of little use without the capacity to refine it.
Concentration as a strategic risk: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions, leaving India open to supply disruptions.
GS2 · India–China / GS3 · Economy
China's hold over mineral processing turns supply chains into tools of pressure, so diversification is national security.
Capex support to start a domestic base: a 30% capital subsidy for four plants (two lithium, two nickel) aims to turn ores into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered from nickel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for processing plants target the costliest, riskiest link in India's mineral value chain.
Clean-energy and strategic sectors depend on it: the minerals feed electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Energy / Defence industry
Without lithium, nickel and cobalt, India's EV and battery ambitions rest on imported inputs.
Cluster approach: processing parks in four states, each built as an ecosystem for one mineral, backed by a planned stockpile under the National Critical Minerals Mission.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Industrial policy
Mineral-specific parks link resource geography to industry, and a strategic stockpile insures against shocks.
keywords: Refining ores into high-purity chemicals used by battery and electronics makers
India's critical mineral challenge is mid-stream: refining, not just mining.
Using dominance over a resource to pressure other countries
China's control of mineral processing shows how supply chains can be weaponised in trade disputes.
A government reserve held to ride out supply disruptions
A critical mineral stockpile works like a strategic oil reserve for the battery age.
Building each stage of production at home
Localising the mineral value chain cuts import dependence from mine to battery.
Industrial parks placed near the raw material they use
Odisha's nickel and Gujarat's heavy rare earths show resource-based clustering in practice.
data: Allocation committed for a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme, 2024-25 to 2030-31
National Critical Minerals Mission (Government of India), via IE
The government has committed Rs 500 crore (2024-25 to 2030-31) for a critical mineral stockpile under the NCMM.
examples: Four mineral-specific processing parks
Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for rare earths, Odisha for nickel, Maharashtra for lithium
GS1 · Distribution of resources · GS3 · Industrial policy
Matching parks to state resources (Odisha's nickel, Gujarat's heavy rare earths) is a model of resource-based industrialisation.

GS4
GS2 · India–China · GS3 · Economy · GS4 · Ethics in IR
China's use of mineral processing as leverage is a clear example of economic interdependence turned into coercion.
Odisha as a gateway for imported nickel
Eastern location suits imports from Indonesia
GS1 · Location of industries · GS2 · Act East
Odisha's eastern coast lets India process nickel imported from Indonesia, linking resources to the Act East region.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges for India as the world moves from free trade to protectionism; how to meet them.
Rationale, achievements and improvements of the PLI scheme.
Why India's mining contributes little to GDP despite its Gondwana origin.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Mineral questions began in physical geography (resource distribution, mining's low GDP share, 2017–2022) and industrial location (2019, 2020). From 2024 the frame shifted to supply chains and geopolitics: India as an alternative to China (2024), protectionism and industrial incentives such as PLI (2025).
trend.watch: Supply-chain resilience and China-plus-one questions are rising since 2024, while mining's environmental cost was asked again in 2025. Critical minerals sit where these meet, so expect a direct question soon.
focus: Industrial policy tools: PLI, capex subsidies, parks
Resource geography and location of processing
Environmental cost of mining and processing

potential: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains. (15 marks)
Why has India remained import-dependent for critical minerals despite its resource base? Examine the role of processing capacity. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains.

answer.t: In November 2026 the Union Cabinet is set to consider a Rs 2,800-crore capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing, as India remains almost fully import-dependent for key critical minerals.

pts.t: Lithium, nickel and cobalt are core to Li-ion batteries for EVs and grid storage.
pts.ex: Needed for India's 500 GW non-fossil goal.

pts.t: Smartphones, semiconductors and electronics depend on these minerals.
Defence systems and speciality steels need rare earths and alloys.
Like oil, control of supply gives power over others.
pts.ex: China's processing dominance used in trade tensions.

pts.t: India relies almost completely on imports for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
Even where ore exists, India lacks refining capacity to make battery-grade compounds.
Global processing is concentrated in China, which has curbed exports of some minerals in the past.
pts.ex: Export curbs on gallium and germanium (2023).

pts.t: Large parts of India's mineral potential remain unexplored.
Processing plants are costly and technology-intensive, deterring private investment.
Mining and chemical processing can damage land, water and local communities.
30% capital subsidy for lithium and nickel plants under the proposed scheme.
A mission-mode approach to exploration, processing and overseas assets, with a planned stockpile.
pts.ex: Rs 500 crore committed for stockpiling (2024-25 to 2030-31).

pts.t: Ecosystems in four states matched to their resources.
pts.ex: Odisha for nickel, Gujarat and AP for rare earths.

pts.t: Secure supplies abroad through state firms and partners.
pts.ex: KABIL; India's membership of the Minerals Security Partnership.

pts.t: Recover minerals from used batteries and e-waste to reduce fresh demand.
Strict environmental norms and benefit-sharing with mining communities.

answer.t: Just as oil security shaped the last century, building domestic processing, diverse partners and a strategic stockpile will decide India's energy and strategic autonomy in this one.

title: Misri to visit Nepal tomorrow, set stage for Balen's likely trip to India this month
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Bilateral agreements · GS3 › Infrastructure: energy (hydropower), connectivity; Disaster management
summary: Foreign Secretary Misri visits Nepal to prepare for PM Balen Shah's likely India visit, with connectivity, hydropower, investment and a trade-treaty update on the agenda after months of strain.
ideas: Repairing ties: after Nepal's PM declined to meet India's Ambassador and the Foreign Secretary's May visit was cancelled, visits by Nepal's Finance Minister and a ruling-party leader began a course correction.
GS2 · India–Nepal
India–Nepal ties show how sustained engagement can repair a relationship after political friction.
Disaster diplomacy builds goodwill: after the August 26 flash flood, India sent humanitarian aid, emergency power support and Bailey bridges, and Nepal's PM thanked India.
GS2 · Neighbourhood First / GS3 · Disaster management
India's quick flood relief to Nepal shows humanitarian assistance as a tool of neighbourhood diplomacy.
Connectivity at the core: roads, railways, air routes and power transmission lines top the agenda.
GS2 · Connectivity / GS3 · Infrastructure
Cross-border connectivity turns geography into shared growth between India and Nepal.
Clean energy as a shared asset: Nepal's large hydropower plans, through run-of-river and storage projects, make power trade central to the partnership.
GS3 · Energy / GS2 · Regional cooperation
Hydropower trade can make Nepal a clean-energy partner for India's grid.

Economic partnership beyond aid: Nepal seeks Indian investment, digitalisation, green manufacturing and tourism, and both sides will discuss updating the trade treaty to cover services, investment protection and profit repatriation.
GS2 · Bilateral agreements
Updating the trade treaty would move India–Nepal ties from aid to investment and services.
keywords: Flood relief and connectivity projects put Neighbourhood First into practice in Nepal.
Using relief to build trust between states
India's flood aid to Nepal is disaster diplomacy that rebuilt goodwill.
Generating power from river flow with little storage
Run-of-river and storage projects underpin Nepal's hydropower ambitions.
Cross-border power trade can integrate South Asia's grids.

GS4

GS2 · India and its neighbourhood
India–Nepal ties show patient diplomacy outlasting political friction.
pyqs: China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition.
How domestic factors shape foreign policy towards a neighbour.
Project Mausam and India's neighbourhood outreach.

trend.t: Neighbourhood questions moved from domestic factors in foreign policy (Sri Lanka, 2013) and the Maldives (2013, 2024) to Sri Lanka's crisis (2022) and China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition (2026). Hydropower technology came in GS3 (2013).
trend.watch: Small neighbours, with China's role in the background, keep returning. Prepare India's tools: connectivity, energy trade, disaster relief and economic partnership, with Nepal as an example.
focus: Connectivity and energy trade with neighbours
Managing political friction with small neighbours

potential: "Connectivity and clean energy can anchor India's relations with Nepal beyond political cycles." Discuss. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Connectivity and clean energy can anchor India's relations with Nepal beyond political cycles." Discuss.

answer.t: Foreign Secretary Misri's Nepal visit, preparing for PM Balen Shah's India trip, puts roads, railways, power lines and hydropower at the centre after months of friction.

pts.t: Power trade and transit create mutual dependence.
Roads and rail serve citizens on both sides.
Nepal's hydropower can feed India's grid.
Connectivity aids disaster relief.
pts.ex: Bailey bridges after the August flood.

pts.t: Leaders' snubs disrupted engagement.
Past delays bred distrust.
Competing infrastructure offers.
Services and investment not covered.
Complete projects on schedule.
Cover services and investment protection.
Regular high-level exchanges.

answer.t: Roads, rails and power lines can outlast governments; delivering them on time is India's best diplomacy in Nepal.

title: PM: India to add 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity in the next 10-11 years
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Climate change; Investment models · GS2 › International agreements (Paris Agreement)
summary: At the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, the PM set a goal of adding 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in 10–11 years, noting India met its Paris target of half its capacity from non-fossil sources five years early.
evolution: Editorial: E100 alone will not secure energy; diesel dominates oil demand.
Editorial page: energy security depends on electrification and how we do it.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity addition goal for the next decade.
ideas: Early delivery on Paris: India pledged that half its installed power capacity would be non-fossil and met it in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
GS2 · Paris Agreement / GS3 · Climate
Meeting the Paris non-fossil capacity target five years early strengthens India's credibility in climate negotiations.
A bigger next step: the PM announced 500 GW of new non-fossil capacity over the next 10–11 years, calling the target difficult but achievable.
GS3 · Energy transition
India's new 500 GW goal signals that the energy transition is moving from targets met to scale-up.
Clean energy as energy security: the PM said clean-energy investment helped India avert a worse energy crisis during the West Asia war.
GS3 · Energy security / GS2 · Foreign policy
Domestic clean power insulates India from fossil-fuel shocks abroad.
Investment drives the shift: the PM cited large flows into renewables over the past decade and big opportunities ahead.
GS3 · Investment
Sustained private investment is what turns renewable targets into installed capacity.
Capacity is not yet generation: a majority of installed capacity is non-fossil, but intermittent sources need storage, grids and flexible supply to deliver reliable power.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Installed capacity must be matched by storage and transmission to become reliable clean electricity.
keywords: A country's climate pledge under the Paris Agreement
India's early achievement of its NDC capacity target shows climate action matching commitment.

trend.t: Renewable questions moved from status and targets (2016) and solar costs (2015, 2020) to whether India will meet 50% renewables by 2030 (2022) and energy independence through clean technology by 2047 (2025). In 2026 the frame became energy security with growth and sustainability.
trend.watch: Renewable targets and energy security now come almost every year. Prepare the Paris target met early, the next goals, and the challenges of storage and grids.

potential: "India's energy transition has moved from setting targets to building systems." Examine with reference to renewable energy. (15 marks)
What challenges must India overcome to add 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in the next decade? (10 marks)

practice.q: What challenges must India overcome to add 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in the next decade?

answer.t: India has 308 GW of non-fossil capacity, 55.1% of the total (CEA), and met its Paris capacity target in 2025; the PM now seeks 500 GW more in 10–11 years.

pts.t: Solar and wind need batteries and pumped hydro for evening and night demand.

answer.t: Having met its Paris target early, India's next test is turning capacity into reliable, round-the-clock clean power.

title: Energy security depends on if we electrify, and how we do it
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Neha Dhingra, CLASP)
syllabus: GS3 › Energy infrastructure; Conservation; Industrial policy (MSMEs) · GS2 › Energy security and foreign policy; Statutory bodies (BEE, BIS) · GS1 › Effects of globalisation on Indian society · GS4 › Innovation in public service
summary: After the Hormuz disruption hit India's LPG supply, the writer argues that electrifying industrial heat (heat pumps) and kitchens (induction) cuts import exposure, if standards and domestic supply come first.
ideas: A far-off war reached Indian kitchens: when Hormuz shipping stalled in March, families queued for cooking gas; the writer notes India imports about 60% of its LPG, nearly 90% of it via the strait.
GS2 · Energy security / GS1 · Globalisation
India's LPG dependence on one chokepoint shows how a distant conflict becomes a domestic crisis within weeks.

Electrification is a security strategy: in NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario, electricity's share of final energy rises from 21% to 60% by 2070 and the fuel import bill falls from about 4% of GDP to 0.2%.
GS3 · Energy transition
Electrification turns India's clean power base into energy security by replacing imported fuel with domestic electricity.

Industrial heat is the lowest-hanging fruit: factories burn coal, oil and gas on site for much of their energy; electrifying it cuts imports, decarbonises industry and helps exporters meet the EU's CBAM.
GS3 · Industry / Climate
Electrifying industrial heat cuts fuel imports, decarbonises industry and protects exports from carbon border taxes.

How we electrify matters: a heat pump, an air conditioner in reverse, gives 2.5 to 4 units of heat per unit of electricity against at most one from an electric boiler; much MSME heat is below 250°C, within its range.
GS3 · Energy efficiency / MSMEs
Heat pumps meet low-temperature industrial heat with a fraction of the electricity, sparing the grid new capacity.

Cost, confidence and supply hold the market back: high upfront cost, efficiency claims tested under foreign standards, and dependence on Chinese imports; Indian standards, BIS certification and a star label should come before demand surges.
GS3 · Industrial policy / GS2 · Regulatory bodies
Standards and labels before a demand surge, plus domestic manufacturing, keep electrification from importing new dependencies.
keywords: Reliance on one narrow sea route for vital imports
LPG's chokepoint dependence on Hormuz makes cooking fuel a strategic vulnerability.
Switching heat, cooking and transport from fuels to electricity

Electrification must not swap a fuel dependence for an equipment dependence.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewable targets and sources (2013, 2015, 2016, 2022) to energy security as a strategic question, in GS2 foreign policy (2017, 2025) and GS3 challenges (2026). The newest asks how clean technology can give energy independence by 2047 (2025).
trend.watch: Energy security came in 2025 and 2026 in both papers, and the angle is shifting from adding supply to cutting dependence. Prepare electrification, efficiency and supply-chain risk together; see also the 31 October E100 card.
focus: Clean-tech manufacturing and dependence on imports

answer.t: Electrification is the most practical path to energy security, provided India builds standards and factories before demand surges, so it does not swap a fuel dependence for an equipment one.
